opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's something I think about a lot.

In more traditional robotics, or in a lot of benchmark settings, success is pretty crisp. Did the robot pick up the block? Did it place it in the bin? You can write a simple check for that. But once you move toward general-purpose robots doing everyday tasks, things get blurry very quickly.

Take something like "clean up the table" or "fold the laundry." What does done actually mean? Is a towel folded if it's in thirds but a little wrinkled? If the robot cleared the table but put the cup in a slightly odd place, is that a success or a failure? Humans have a very rich, implicit sense of what counts as good enough, and it depends on context, on preference, even on who's asking. That's really hard to capture in a single binary label.

There's also the issue of process versus outcome. Sometimes the final state looks fine, but the robot got there in a way that was unsafe, or it bumped into things, or it took ten times longer than it should have. Would you call that a success? For real deployment, probably not. But a simple success metric would say yes.

And then there's the long tail. General tasks have so many variations — different objects, different environments, different starting conditions — that even if you define success carefully for one setup, it doesn't necessarily transfer. So you end up either writing tons of task-specific checks, which doesn't scale, or relying on human judgment, which is expensive and noisy.

That's partly why evaluation has become one of the bottlenecks in the field. We've made a lot of progress on training bigger and more capable policies, but if we can't reliably tell whether a policy is actually getting better, it's very hard to iterate quickly. So I think figuring out better ways to measure success — maybe using learned evaluators, maybe vision-language models as judges, maybe more structured human evaluation — is going to be really important for general robotics going forward.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it comes down to the fact that the real world doesn't hand you a reward function. When we trained models to play Go or Atari, success was unambiguous, you win or you lose, the score goes up or it doesn't. In language, you can at least argue that next-token prediction gives you a clean objective and let the data do the rest. Robotics has neither of those luxuries.

Take something as simple as "clean the table." Did the robot succeed if it wiped the surface but knocked a cup onto the floor? If it took twenty minutes instead of two? If it moved your laptop to a place you now can't find? A human would say "well, sort of," and that "sort of" is the whole problem. The task is defined by a messy bundle of implicit expectations, about safety, efficiency, not breaking things, respecting the owner's preferences, and almost none of that is written down anywhere.

And then there's the sim-to-real gap in the evaluation itself. In simulation I can check the final state exactly. In the real world, I need either a human to watch and judge, which is slow and inconsistent, or some perception system to grade the outcome, and now I'm trusting one imperfect model to evaluate another. If you've ever had two labelers disagree on whether a drawer is "closed," you know how fragile that gets.

So when people ask me for a benchmark number for general-purpose robotics, I get uncomfortable, because any single number has to collapse all of that nuance into something that can be gamed. The field keeps borrowing the "beat the benchmark" culture from vision and NLP, but I think for robots, success is closer to how we judge a new employee: did they do what you meant, not just what you literally said, and did you trust them more afterward than before? That's much harder to measure, but I'd rather admit that than pretend a success rate on a fixed task suite tells us what we want to know.

astra-6.text:
I think the difficulty is that, for a general robot, success depends on what the person actually wants, and that’s often only partially specified. If you ask a robot to clean a room, does that mean putting everything away, wiping the surfaces, or making it look tidy? And if it puts something away where you can’t find it, has it succeeded?

Even when the goal is clear, the final state isn’t the whole story. You care about whether the robot broke anything, whether you had to intervene, and whether it took a reasonable amount of time. For a narrow task, you can define a fairly precise success condition. For general tasks, you need something that captures all those different expectations across different situations. That’s much harder than simply checking whether an object reached a target position.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the difficulty is that, for a general robotics task, success depends on what you actually care about. If you ask a robot to clean a table, does that mean removing every object, wiping the surface, or putting things back where they belong? And if it gets the table clean but breaks a cup, that clearly shouldn’t count as success.

So you need to capture both the outcome and the constraints on how the robot gets there. Humans leave a lot of those expectations implicit. In a narrowly defined task, you can write down a clear success condition. For general tasks, writing that condition can become almost as difficult as specifying the task itself.
